title: Open Minds 2026
author: Chrys Dougherty
source: chrysdougherty.substack.com (The Active Citizen's Guide to Improving Schools), October 19,
summary: This is the fourth post in Chrys Dougherty's series on educating informed citizens for a liberal democracy, and it asks what schools can do to cultivate open-mindedness. He defines open-minded people by three attributes: intellectual curiosity, intellectual humility, and a belief in intellectual pluralism. Society's system of free inquiry does not need every individual to be open-minded, but a population that values diversity of thought is more likely to protect free speech, less likely to treat opponents as enemies, and quicker to spread good ideas. Dougherty is careful to say that open-mindedness is not credulity and must rest on a knowledge-rich curriculum and evidence-based reasoning. He then proposes three things students should learn: the history of free inquiry and free speech, the educational value of taking opposing views seriously, and how to understand and work with people one disagrees with. He closes with ground rules for productive discussion and a short reading list including Rauch, Norberg, and the Chicago principles.
points: Open-mindedness is defined by three attributes (curiosity, humility, pluralism), which gives schools concrete dispositions to cultivate rather than a vague virtue.
Dougherty argues that a society's free inquiry can work without universal open-mindedness, but a more open-minded population reduces polarization and speeds the diffusion of good ideas.
He insists open-mindedness is not credulity; it must be anchored in knowledge and evidence-based reasoning to slow the spread of bad ideas.
Studying the history of censorship, from Galileo to Soviet genetics, is proposed as part of a knowledge-rich curriculum on free speech.

Being forced to consider opposing views is framed as a desirable difficulty that corrects the illusion of understanding, and classroom ground rules for discussion should be modelled by adults in the community too.
quotes: People with open minds are willing to consider ideas and evidence that go against their preferred beliefs.
Open-mindedness is not credulity; it must include a strong grounding in knowledge and evidence-based reasoning to slow the spread of bad ideas.
In general, human flourishing tended to occur when society was open to knowledge and ideas from many sources and those ideas were not restricted by a central authority.
Having to consider limitations in your own understanding and think seriously about opinions you disagree with is a desirable difficulty

People often have the illusion of understanding things better than they do. As a consequence, they benefit from having their ideas questioned: How do you know this? Why isn’t this competing idea true instead?
Ground rules for productive discussion emphasize listening to and understanding the views of others and beginning with the assumption that participants are acting in good faith.
Parents, teachers, and active citizens should follow these rules in their own behaviors in public meetings and events.
